narrative:
The model estimates a 35% chance that you will not pass your final year, which is high enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a safety measure.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your reason for choosing the school, your history of past failures, and the amount of free time you have after school. Your choice of the school based on its reputation was the single biggest influence, and it actually worked in your favor by pulling the prediction toward passing. Most students who passed also chose the school for its reputation or its course offerings, so this decision aligned you with successful peers.

However, having one past class failure pushed the prediction toward failing more strongly than any other factor. Among students who passed, the average number of prior failures was zero, so even a single earlier setback stood out as a warning sign to the model.

Your low amount of free time after school also nudged the outcome toward failing. While this might seem counter-intuitive, students who passed typically reported medium or high free time, suggesting that very limited downtime may reflect an overloaded schedule that leaves little room to catch up on difficult material.

To improve, focus first on addressing any remaining gaps from that past failure. Creating a realistic weekly study schedule that gives you consistent review time, even if it means slightly adjusting your free hours, can help turn the 35% risk into a passing grade.
